newsitem.title: UK: British Conservative manifesto banks on tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: British Conservative manifesto banks on tax cuts.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives on Wednesday launched their manifesto for a May 1 general election, including a pledge to introduce tax cuts to help make Britain "the best place in the world to live".

Prime Minister John Major, trying to dispel a widespread public perception that the Conservatives have run out of ideas after 18 consecutive years in power, vowed to cut the basic rate of income tax to 20 percent from 23 percent.
He also promised tax breaks for people who stayed at home to take care of childen or sick relatives, saying the proposal would strengthen family values and help those in need.

Braced by an opinion poll showing the Labour opposition's lead had fallen to 14 percentage points, Major boasted Conservative governments since 1979 had been "among the most successful in British peacetime history".
"Why, then, do we still need a Conservative government? Because resting on what we have achieved is not enough," he wrote in the foreword to the manifesto.
"To stand still is to fall back. Our goal must be for Britain to be the best place in the world to live."

But Labour quickly counter-attacked. Its economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, said the Conservative tax cut pledge could cost more than five billion pounds ($8 billion) a year, four times the sum that Major estimated.
Brown condemned Major's promise to introduce it in the second year of a new government as "reckless".
"The question Mr Major must answer is: "Where is the money for his tax changes coming from? Why is he risking economic recovery and higher interest rates by a reckless and desperate set of promises?"

The Conservatives, racked by internal strife over the country's future within the European Union and damaged by sleaze allegations against several of their members of parliament, are battling to get back on terms with a resurgent Labour Party under moderate Tony Blair.
A poll in the Guardian newspaper gave them some hope this could be achieved, showing Labour's opinion poll lead had slipped by four percentage points over the past month to 14 points.

However, even this lead would give Blair an overall majority of 137 seats in an expanded 659-member House of Commons which Britons will elect in just over four weeks' time. Labour needs a swing of 4.3 percent to win the election.

The Conservatives won the last election in 1992 with a majority of 21 in the then 651-seat House of Commons (lower house), but this was reduced by byelections, defections and deaths of members to a minority of three when parliament was wound up last month.

The Conservative manifesto set out radical plans to involve the private sector in British pension arrangements, an extension of privatisation to parts of the postal service and to London's underground railway, and increased funding every year for the National Health Service.
However, attempting to bridge the gulf in the party over relations with the European Union, it was cautious about the prospects of Britain signing up to the bloc's planned single urrency.

Responding to calls from Eurosceptic MPs for the party to rule out British participation, it said merely that a new Conservative government would not legislate in the first session of a new parliament on the issue.
